cards.question: Why does machine learning rely so heavily on linear algebra for dimensionality reduction techniques such as PCA?
cards.answer: PCA uses eigenvectors and eigenvalues to find lower-dimensional representations, or new features, that are combinations of the existing ones.
distractors: PCA uses a nearest-neighbour search to pick the most informative attributes.
PCA uses a cost function between observations and predictions to remove noisy attributes.
PCA uses one-out-of-K encoding to merge correlated attributes.

cards.question: Which of these is an example of 'model formulation' with vectors and matrices?
cards.answer: A linear model written as f(x; w) = wᵀx̃.
distractors: Storing a dataset with one data point per row.
Rotating a shape by multiplying it with a rotation matrix.
Computing the mean of every column of the data matrix.

cards.question: Why is linear algebra notation useful for the optimization of modern ML models?
cards.answer: Modern ML models rely heavily on gradient methods, and gradients are conveniently represented as vectors and matrices, for example a Jacobian or Hessian.
distractors: Optimization only needs the data matrix X and never uses gradients.
Matrices guarantee that every optimization problem has a single global optimum.
Gradients are scalars, so linear algebra is needed only for the data.

cards.question: What is an M-dimensional vector space, and what closure property does it have?
cards.answer: It is Rᴹ, the set of all M-dimensional real vectors, and it is closed under linear combinations.
distractors: It is the set of all N × M matrices, and it is closed under matrix multiplication only.
It is the set of all unit vectors in Rᴹ, and it is closed under addition.
It is any set of M data points, and it is closed under taking the mean.

cards.question: How can a vector x = [x1, x2, x3]ᵀ in R³ be written using the standard basis vectors e1 = (1,0,0), e2 = (0,1,0) and e3 = (0,0,1)?
cards.answer: As the linear combination x = x1·e1 + x2·e2 + x3·e3.
distractors: As the product x = e1·e2·e3 scaled by the norm of x.
As x = e1 + e2 + e3, independent of x1, x2 and x3.

cards.question: What is the span of vectors v1, ..., vn?
cards.answer: The set of all linear combinations z = a1v1 + a2v2 + ... + anvn, which is a subspace.
distractors: The set of all vectors orthogonal to v1, ..., vn.
The set containing only v1, ..., vn themselves.
The single vector obtained by adding v1, ..., vn.

cards.question: What does a subspace generalize?
cards.answer: The concept of a line or plane (through the origin) in a higher-dimensional space.
distractors: The concept of a distance measure between two data points.
The concept of a matrix inverse.
The concept of a covariance between two attributes.

cards.question: When are the vectors v1, ..., vn linearly independent?
cards.answer: When 0 = a1v1 + ... + anvn implies that a1 = a2 = ... = an = 0.
distractors: When all the vectors have unit length.
When vᵢᵀvⱼ = 0 for every pair i ≠ j.
When each vector can be written as a linear combination of the others.

cards.question: What is a basis for a vector space or subspace V?
cards.answer: A set of n linearly independent vectors whose span is V.
distractors: Any set of vectors lying in V, even if linearly dependent.
A set of unit vectors that sum to the zero vector.
The set of eigenvalues of V.

cards.question: When is a basis called orthonormal?
cards.answer: When the basis vectors are pairwise orthogonal (vᵢᵀvⱼ = 0 for i ≠ j) and each has unit length (||vᵢ|| = 1).
distractors: When the basis vectors are linearly dependent but of unit length.
When the basis vectors are orthogonal but may have any length.
When the basis vectors have unit length but may point in any direction.

cards.question: If the basis vectors are collected as the columns of a matrix V and the basis is orthonormal, which equation holds?
cards.answer: VᵀV = I.
distractors: VᵀV = 0.
V + Vᵀ = I.
VᵀV = the covariance matrix of the data.

cards.question: How are the basis vectors arranged in the basis matrix V = span(v1, ..., vn)?
cards.answer: As the columns of V.
distractors: As the rows of V.
As the diagonal of V.
As the eigenvalues of V.

cards.question: The span of two linearly independent vectors in R³ is geometrically what?
cards.answer: A plane through the origin.
distractors: A single line through the origin.
All of R³.
A single point at the origin.

cards.question: What is the cosine of the angle φ between vectors v and x?
cards.answer: cos(φ) = vᵀx / (||x||₂ ||v||₂).
distractors: cos(φ) = ||x||₂ ||v||₂ / vᵀx.
cos(φ) = vᵀx · ||x||₂ ||v||₂.

cards.question: What is the length of the projection of x onto a direction v?
cards.answer: p = ||x||₂ cos(φ) = vᵀx / ||v||₂.
distractors: p = ||x||₂ sin(φ).
p = vᵀx · ||v||₂.

cards.question: What does the projection length simplify to when v is a unit vector?
cards.answer: p = vᵀx.
distractors: p = vᵀx / ||x||₂.
p = vvᵀx.

cards.question: What is the length of the projection of x = [3, 4]ᵀ onto the unit vector v = [0.6, 0.8]ᵀ?
How do you project an M-dimensional point x onto the subspace given by an orthonormal basis matrix V (M × n)?
cards.answer: bᵀ = xᵀV, which gives an n-dimensional coordinate vector b.
distractors: b = Vᵀ + x, which gives an M-dimensional vector.
b = VVᵀ, which does not depend on x.
bᵀ = xᵀx, which gives a scalar.

cards.question: Given the projection coordinates b, how is the 'reconstruction' of x in the original space found?
cards.answer: x' = Vb.
distractors: x' = Vᵀb.
x' = b / V.
x' = bᵀb.

cards.question: V = [[1,0],[0,0],[0,1]] is used to project x = [x1, x2, x3]ᵀ via xᵀV. What is the result?
cards.answer: [x1, x3], which keeps x1 and x3 and drops x2.
distractors: [x1, x2], which keeps x1 and x2 and drops x3.
[x1 + x3], a single scalar.
[x1, 0, x3], a 3-dimensional vector.

cards.question: What does Av = λv say about v, for a square matrix A?
cards.answer: v is an eigenvector of A with eigenvalue λ.
distractors: v is a singular vector and λ is its norm.
v is the inverse of A scaled by λ.
v is orthogonal to A with angle λ.

cards.question: What do we know about the eigenvectors and eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix A = Aᵀ?
cards.answer: It has orthogonal eigenvectors and real eigenvalues.
distractors: It has complex eigenvalues and non-orthogonal eigenvectors.
It has only one eigenvector.
It has orthogonal eigenvectors, but its eigenvalues can be complex.

cards.question: What is the goal of PCA for high-dimensional data?
cards.answer: To find a lower-dimensional representation of the high-dimensional data by projecting it onto a subspace.
distractors: To find the class label of each data point using its nearest neighbours.
To increase the number of attributes to make classes separable.
To remove outliers from the dataset.

cards.question: Which criterion does PCA use to choose a good projection direction?
cards.answer: It selects the projection that maximizes the variance of the projected data.
distractors: It selects the projection that minimizes the variance of the projected data.
It selects the projection that maximizes the number of misclassified points.
It selects the projection along the attribute with the largest mean.

cards.question: In 1D PCA with centre m and unit direction v, how is a point x reconstructed from its projection?
cards.answer: x' = v·p + m, where p = vᵀ(x − m).
distractors: x' = v·p − m, where p = vᵀx.
x' = p / v + m, where p = (x − m)ᵀx.
x' = p·m, where p = vᵀm.

cards.question: In the PCA derivation, how is the variance of the projected data b_i = x_iᵀv written?
cards.answer: Var[b] = (1/(N−1)) vᵀX̃ᵀX̃v, where X̃ is the centered data matrix.
distractors: Var[b] = (1/N) vᵀXXᵀv using the uncentered data matrix.
Var[b] = vᵀv / (N − 1).

cards.question: Why do we constrain ||v||₂ = 1 when maximizing the variance of the projection?
cards.answer: Without it, the variance could be increased arbitrarily by scaling v, so we only want to optimize the direction.
distractors: Because eigenvectors only exist for unit vectors.
Because the data has already been standardized to unit length.
Because the mean of the projected data must be zero.

cards.question: What type of problem do we obtain after solving the constrained maximization of the variance with a Lagrange multiplier?
cards.answer: An eigenvalue problem: (1/(N−1)) X̃ᵀX̃ v = λv.
distractors: A linear regression problem: X̃v = y.
A nearest-neighbour problem: v = argmin ||x − v||.
A matrix inversion problem: v = (X̃ᵀX̃)⁻¹.

cards.question: At the optimum, what is the variance of the data projected onto the eigenvector v?
cards.answer: It equals the corresponding eigenvalue λ.
distractors: It equals 1, because v has unit length.
It equals the square root of the eigenvalue.
It equals 0, because the data is centered.

cards.question: Which eigenvector of (1/(N−1)) X̃ᵀX̃ gives the first principal component?
cards.answer: The one with the largest eigenvalue.
distractors: The one with the smallest eigenvalue.
The one whose entries are all positive.
The one corresponding to the attribute with the largest mean.

cards.question: What matrix is (1/(N−1)) X̃ᵀX̃ for a centered data matrix X̃?
cards.answer: The empirical covariance matrix of the data.
distractors: The correlation matrix of the data.
The matrix of pairwise distances between data points.
The projection matrix onto the first principal component.

cards.question: What is the shape of the covariance matrix computed as (1/(N−1)) X̃ᵀX̃ for an N × M data matrix?
cards.answer: M × M.
distractors: N × N.
N × M.

cards.question: In the SVD X = UΣVᵀ of an N × M matrix X, what are the shapes and properties of U, Σ and V?
cards.answer: U is N × N orthonormal, Σ is N × M diagonal, and V is M × M orthonormal.
distractors: U is N × M diagonal, Σ is N × N orthonormal, and V is M × M orthonormal.
U is N × N diagonal, Σ is N × M orthonormal, and V is M × M diagonal.
U is N × N orthonormal, Σ is M × M diagonal, and V is N × M orthonormal.

cards.question: Which identities hold for the orthonormal matrices in the SVD?
cards.answer: UᵀU = I (N × N) and VᵀV = I (M × M).
distractors: UᵀU = Σ and VᵀV = Σ.
UUᵀ = 0 and VVᵀ = 0.
U = V and Σ = I.

cards.question: How are the columns of V related to the covariance matrix of the centered data X̃?
cards.answer: They are its eigenvectors, because (1/(N−1)) X̃ᵀX̃ vᵢ = (1/(N−1)) σᵢ² vᵢ.
distractors: They are the rows of the covariance matrix.
They are its eigenvalues.
They are the columns of U scaled by the singular values.

cards.question: What is the eigenvalue of (1/(N−1)) X̃ᵀX̃ associated with the right singular vector vᵢ?
cards.answer: σᵢ² / (N−1), where σᵢ is the i-th singular value of X̃.
distractors: σᵢ² · (N−1).
σᵢ² / N, using the biased estimate.

cards.question: In the SVD derivation of PCA, why does X̃ᵀX̃ vᵢ simplify to σᵢ² vᵢ?
cards.answer: Because Vᵀvᵢ is the i-th unit vector eᵢ, and ΣᵀΣ is diagonal with entries σⱼ², giving X̃ᵀX̃ vᵢ = V ΣᵀΣ eᵢ = σᵢ² vᵢ.
distractors: Because U is the identity matrix for centered data.
Because Σ has ones on its diagonal for centered data.
Because X̃ᵀ = X̃ for centered data.

cards.question: What is the first step of PCA?
cards.answer: Subtract the column-wise mean m from the data matrix, so that x̃ᵢ = xᵢ − m.
distractors: Apply the SVD to the raw data matrix.
Select the K first columns of V.
Project the data onto the first K eigenvectors.

cards.question: After centering the data, what are the next steps of PCA?
cards.answer: Apply the SVD X̃ = UΣVᵀ and select the first K columns of V as the principal directions.
distractors: Compute the nearest neighbours of every point and average them.
Sort the data by the first attribute and take the K first rows.
Invert X̃ and select the K largest entries.

cards.question: Why might you also standardize the data before PCA?
cards.answer: Standardizing puts attributes on a comparable scale, so that attributes with large scales do not dominate the variance.
distractors: Standardizing guarantees the principal components have unit length.
Standardizing removes all correlations between attributes.
Standardizing makes the data orthonormal, so no SVD is needed.

cards.question: How should nominal attributes be handled before applying PCA, according to the lecture?
cards.answer: They can be represented with one-out-of-K encoding, although this is not ideal.
distractors: They are assigned consecutive integers, which is the ideal representation.
They must be removed from the data.
They are replaced by their mean.

cards.question: How are the PCA coordinates (projection) B of the data onto the first K components computed?
cards.answer: B = X̃ V₍K₎, an N × K matrix.
distractors: B = V₍K₎ X̃, a K × N matrix.
B = X V₍K₎ᵀ, an N × M matrix.
B = Σ V₍K₎, a K × K matrix.

cards.question: How is a PCA coordinate vector bᵢ reconstructed to the original, non-centered space using K components?
cards.answer: x'ᵢ = V₍K₎ bᵢ + m.
distractors: x'ᵢ = V₍K₎ᵀ bᵢ − m.
x'ᵢ = bᵢ / V₍K₎.
x'ᵢ = Σ₍K₎ bᵢ.

cards.question: How can the i-th principal component of the centered data be written using the SVD?
cards.answer: bᵢ = X̃ vᵢ = uᵢ σᵢ.
distractors: bᵢ = X̃ uᵢ = vᵢ σᵢ.
bᵢ = X̃ᵀ vᵢ = uᵢ / σᵢ.
bᵢ = vᵢ σᵢ².

cards.question: What is true about the ordering of the singular values in Σ?
cards.answer: They are sorted largest first, σ₁ ≥ σ₂ ≥ ... ≥ σ_M ≥ 0.
distractors: They are sorted smallest first, σ₁ ≤ σ₂ ≤ ... ≤ σ_M.
They are in no particular order.
They are all equal to 1 for centered data.

cards.question: What do the singular values tell us in PCA?
cards.answer: How much variability is explained by the corresponding component: the first explains most, the second most of the remainder, and so on.
distractors: The class labels of the corresponding data points.
The mean of the data along each principal direction.
The number of data points that project onto each component.

cards.question: How much variance is retained by a reconstruction X' using the first K components?
distractors: (Σ_{i≤K} σᵢ) / (Σ_{i≤M} σᵢ).
K / M.
σ_K² / σ₁².

cards.question: What fraction of the variance does the i-th principal component explain?
cards.answer: σᵢ² / Σⱼ σⱼ².
distractors: σᵢ / Σⱼ σⱼ.
σᵢ² / σ₁².

cards.question: Why is the squared Frobenius norm of the centered data matrix equal to the sum of the squared singular values?
cards.answer: Because ||X̃||²_F = trace(X̃ᵀX̃) = trace(UΣVᵀVΣᵀUᵀ) = trace(ΣΣᵀ) = Σᵢ σᵢ², using the orthonormality of U and V.
distractors: Because the Frobenius norm is defined as the largest singular value.
Because ||X̃||²_F is the number of non-zero entries of X̃.
Because the trace of any matrix equals its largest eigenvalue.

cards.question: Which identity about the trace is used in the derivation of the explained variance?
cards.answer: trace(AB) = trace(BA).
distractors: trace(AB) = trace(A) · trace(B).
trace(A) = trace(A⁻¹).
trace(AB) = trace(A) + trace(B).

cards.question: The squared Frobenius norm of a standardized data matrix is 5780.0 and the first singular value is 40.1. What fraction of the variation does the first principal component explain?
cards.answer: Approximately 27.8%, since 40.1² / 5780.0 ≈ 0.278.
distractors: Approximately 0.7%, since 40.1 / 5780.0 ≈ 0.007.
Approximately 55.6%, since 2 · 40.1² / 5780.0 ≈ 0.556.
Approximately 100%, since the first component explains everything.

cards.question: With ||X||²_F = 5780.0 and singular values 40.1, 34.2, 28.1 and 24.8, what fraction of the variation do the first three components account for?
cards.answer: About 61.7%, which is less than 70%.
distractors: About 76.8%, which is more than 70%.
About 27.8%, which is the contribution of the first component alone.
About 10.6%, which is the contribution of the fourth component.

cards.question: With ||X||²_F = 5780.0, how much variation does the fourth principal component with σ₄ = 24.8 explain?
distractors: About 24.8%, since the singular value is a percentage.

cards.question: With ||X||²_F = 5780.0 and σ₂ = 34.2, what fraction does the second component explain?
cards.answer: About 20.2%.
distractors: About 30.0%.
About 34.2%.
About 5.9%.

cards.question: A centered data matrix has exactly four non-zero singular values: 4, 3, 2 and 1. What fraction of the variance is retained by the first two components?
In the Iris PCA example using sepal length, sepal width and petal length, which original attribute dominates the first principal direction v₁ = [−0.39, 0.09, −0.92]?
cards.answer: Petal length, which has the largest absolute coefficient (−0.92).
distractors: Sepal width, which has the only positive coefficient.
Sepal length, which comes first in the vector.
All three attributes contribute equally.

cards.question: In the Iris example, the PCA projection onto the first components was compared with a scatter plot of two original attributes. What was the conclusion?
cards.answer: The PCA projection captures the structure of the data better than a projection onto two of the original attributes.
distractors: The two original attributes separate the classes better than PCA.
Both projections look identical.
PCA fails because it ignores the class labels completely.

cards.question: In the Iris example with mean μ = [5.8, 3.1, 3.8]ᵀ, what does the mean represent in the PCA picture?
cards.answer: The centre of the data, through which the principal directions pass.
distractors: The first principal direction v₁.
The eigenvalue of the first principal component.
The point in the data with the smallest variance.

cards.question: In the liver-disease PCA, AGE, GDR, TB, DB, AP, AlA and AsA have negative coefficients in PC1 while TP, AB and A/G have positive ones. What projection onto PC1 results from high AGE, GDR, TB, DB, AP, AlA, AsA and low TP, AB, A/G?
cards.answer: A negative projection onto PC1.
distractors: A positive projection onto PC1.
A projection of exactly zero.
It cannot be determined from the signs of the coefficients.

cards.question: In the liver-disease PCA, AGE has a negative coefficient in PC2 while most other attributes have positive coefficients (GDR and AP are near zero). What does PC2 mainly discriminate?
cards.answer: Old subjects with low values of the other attributes versus young subjects with high values of those attributes.
distractors: Male subjects versus female subjects.
Subjects with liver disease versus subjects without it.
Subjects with high AGE and high TB versus subjects with low AGE and low TB.

cards.question: Are the principal component directions guaranteed to be orthogonal if the data has been standardized?
cards.answer: Yes, they are always orthogonal, irrespective of preprocessing, since they are the orthonormal columns of V.
distractors: No, standardization makes them non-orthogonal.
Only when the data has not been standardized.
Only the first two are orthogonal.

cards.question: In the liver data plotted on PCA1 and PCA2, observations with low PCA1 and high PCA2 were mostly of which kind?
cards.answer: Subjects with liver disease.
distractors: Subjects without liver disease.
Subjects who are all male.
Subjects whose attributes are all missing.

cards.question: If each handwritten digit image is 28 × 28 pixels and there are N images, what is the shape of the data matrix X?
For a digit PCA with 2 components, a point is reconstructed as x' = V₍K₎ b + m. What are the shapes of V₍K₎, b and m?
cards.answer: V₍K₎ is 784 × 2, b is 2 × 1, and m is 784 × 1.
distractors: V₍K₎ is 2 × 784, b is 784 × 1, and m is 2 × 1.
V₍K₎ is 2 × 2, b is 2 × 1, and m is 2 × 1.

cards.question: When you choose a 2D 'code' b in the PCA plot of digits and reconstruct an image, why might the result look blurry or lack some detail?
cards.answer: Because projecting onto a low-dimensional subspace discards information, so the reconstruction may miss some of the original information.
distractors: Because the reconstruction uses the median instead of the mean.
Because PCA reconstructs only the pixels with the largest values.
Because the mean m is added twice.

cards.question: Each face image in the 'Faces in the wild' example is 86 × 86 pixels with 3 RGB intensities. What is the dimension of one image as a vector?
After stacking 1000 of these face images as vectors, what is the shape of the data matrix?
How does reconstruction quality of digits change when we use K = 2, 5, 20, 50 and 100 principal components?
cards.answer: The reconstruction gets better and closer to the original as more components are used.
distractors: The reconstruction gets worse as more components are used.
The reconstruction is perfect for every K.
The reconstruction quality does not depend on K.

cards.question: How does PCA differ from the Fourier transform as a feature extraction method?
cards.answer: PCA is data driven, with features defined from the data to preserve variance, while the Fourier transform is domain driven, with fixed frequency components suited to, for example, sound analysis.
distractors: PCA is domain driven and the Fourier transform is data driven.
Both are data driven, but the Fourier transform preserves variance.
Both are domain driven, but PCA uses frequencies.

cards.question: In the Fourier transform matrix V⁽ᶠᶠᵀ⁾, what do the components represent, and what does projecting data onto them give?
cards.answer: The components are specific frequencies, and the projection shows to what extent each frequency is present in the data.
distractors: The components are the directions of maximum variance, and the projection gives the explained variance.
The components are one-out-of-K indicators, and the projection gives class labels.
The components are the data points, and the projection gives distances to neighbours.

cards.question: Which matrix rotates a 2D point by an angle θ?
cards.answer: R(θ) = [[cos θ, −sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]].
distractors: S = [[cos θ, 0], [0, sin θ]].
R(θ) = [[sin θ, cos θ], [cos θ, −sin θ]].

cards.question: Which of the following correctly describes the Frobenius norm of a matrix?
cards.answer: ||X||²_F = Σᵢⱼ xᵢⱼ² = trace(XXᵀ) = trace(XᵀX).
distractors: ||X||_F = max over all entries |xᵢⱼ|.
||X||²_F = trace(X)².
||X||_F = Σᵢ xᵢᵢ, the sum of the diagonal.

cards.question: In week 3, what was the main recap from week 2 that PCA builds on?
cards.answer: Summary statistics, vector spaces and distances, and k-nearest neighbours.
distractors: Decision trees and cross-validation.
Bayesian inference and linear models.
Neural networks and optimization.
